title: Sadhna's plea for grace
hook: Sadhna, remembered as a butcher, pleads to be saved by grace (Bilaval, Sadhna, ang 858)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaaiaa: deity, temple and pilgrim, all found in the body. Your line was the body is the temple. What one act of honor did you give it? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

A lifeguard who waits until the swimmer has gone under for good, then rows out with a boat. What use is that? Sadhna asks almost exactly that question, out loud, to God. Tradition remembers him as a butcher, and his hymn sits in the Guru Granth Sahib all the same. That hymn isn't calm. It's urgent, a little bold, and full of arguments. He isn't asking whether grace exists. He's asking for it now.
screen: `A BOAT AFTER THE SWIMMER DROWNS.` → `REMEMBERED AS A BUTCHER.` → `GRACE, AND NOW.`

segments.voice: Sadhna's hymn is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang 858. He argues like someone who knows he can't earn what he's asking for. First argument, in paraphrase: O Guru of the world, what good are Your virtues if my karma isn't wiped away? Why run to a lion for shelter, if a jackal is going to eat you anyway? In other words: if I'm only saved by my own record, why come to You at all? The point of seeking refuge is that the refuge is stronger than what's chasing you. Second argument: the chaatrik, the rainbird of Indian poetry that longs for a single raindrop. For one drop, Sadhna says, the bird suffers; once its life is gone, an ocean is no use to it. Third, the boat. My life is worn out and unsteady, he says; how can I wait? If I drown and die, and then a boat arrives, tell me, who will you put on board? Each picture says the same thing from a new side: grace that comes too late isn't grace. And then everything drops away. In paraphrase: I am nothing, I have nothing, nothing at all is mine. At this moment, protect my honor; Sadhna is Your servant. That's the plea for grace. Not a list of good deeds, because he doesn't claim any. Just an empty pair of hands and a deadline. Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy. Sadhna's hymn is what asking for that glance sounds like when there's nothing left to bargain with.
screen: `THE LION AND THE JACKAL.` · `ONE DROP FOR THE RAINBIRD.` · `A BOAT AFTER DROWNING IS NO USE.` · then, large: `I HAVE NOTHING; SAVE ME NOW.`

segments.voice: The practice: ask for grace once. Use the sit to find the place in your life where effort has run out: a habit you can't break, a relationship you can't fix, a fear you can't argue away. Don't make a case for yourself. Let your hands be empty, like Sadhna's. If you pray, you can ask once, simply, for grace there, in your own words or with the Name. If you don't, simply name it honestly, once, without a plan to fix it. Then breathe, with Waheguru on each breath out if you like. The bell holds the time.
Nadar. The gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy: Sadhna's plea when there was nothing left to bargain with.
Your line: saved by grace. Today, when you hit the place where effort runs out, remember Sadhna's boat, and ask before you go under. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 785 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RAMANAND: WHERE SHALL I GO.`

howItsDone: Sadhna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the Lord's gracious glance, as a gift that can be asked for but never earned or forced.

options: a promise to do better later.
empty hands: I have nothing; save me now.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the gracious glance, the Sikh word for grace that can't be forced or bought.

trapdoor: what you thought: a humble prayer that waits quietly.
what it means: an urgent plea: grace that comes after the drowning is no grace, so save me now.
what a scholar hears: the lion-and-jackal line argues that if karma alone decides, refuge in the Lord would mean nothing.
recall: the Lord the boy pleads with

notes: Hymn paraphrased from memory (tav gun kahaa jagat guraa jau karam na naasai; singh saran kat jaaeeai jau janbuk graasai; ek boond jal kaarne chaatrik dukh paavai; boodh mooe naukaa milai kahu kaahi chadhaavau; main naahee kachh hau nahee kichh aahi na moraa; aausar lajaa raakh lehu sadhnaa jan toraa). Please check each paraphrase.
The hymn's first verse (the man who disguised himself for a king's daughter) is left out deliberately; a Keeper may want it mentioned.
The script avoids saying how many hymns of Sadhna are in the Granth; a Keeper may add it if wanted.
Sadhna as a butcher is tradition, stated as such in the hook.
Nadar is introduced as Sikh teaching (from the Gurus' bani), not as Sadhna's own word; confirm Gurmukhi ਨਦਰਿ.
Editor: cut an unsourced claim about the social standing of Sadhna's trade; removed the third 'if you pray' in the practice.
Audit: the non-praying option asked listeners to 'admit' they need 'help you can't earn', which assumed a belief; softened to naming the place honestly.
